/h1: Does palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 reduce fine lines and wrinkles?
/deck: A 12-week, double-blind, split-face trial of palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 in 93 women: the peptide in the original Matrixyl®, not the two peptides in Matrixyl® 3000.
/definition: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (pal-KTTKS) is the peptide Sederma sells as Matrixyl®, the original version of the ingredient: five amino acids from type I procollagen joined to palmitic acid, a fatty acid. It is a different ingredient from [Matrixyl® 3000](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/matrixyl-3000-research), which pairs palmitoyl tripeptide-1 with palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7.
/answer: In the Robinson 2005 trial, 93 women used a moisturiser with 3 ppm palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 on one side of the face and the same moisturiser without it on the other, twice a day for 12 weeks, without knowing which was which. From week 8, image analysis and expert graders found fine lines and wrinkles reduced more on the peptide side.
/verdict: **Our verdict:** the largest published controlled trial of palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 on its own, with each woman as her own comparison, and the peptide side pulled ahead on fine lines and wrinkles from week 8. The effect was small, the authors worked for Procter & Gamble, and it tested the original Matrixyl®, not Matrixyl® 3000.
/seo_title: Palmitoyl Pentapeptide-4 for Wrinkles: Robinson 2005 Trial
/seo_description: In a split-face trial of 93 women, 3 ppm palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, the original Matrixyl®, reduced fine lines and wrinkles more than placebo from week 8.
/figures/0/note: A moisturiser with the peptide on one side of the face and the same moisturiser without it on the other, twice a day for 12 weeks ([Robinson et al., 2005](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18492182/)).
/figures/1/label: Fine lines ahead of placebo (p ≤ 0.10; size not reported)
/figures/1/note: Image analysis and expert graders both favoured the peptide side at weeks 8 and 12, by the paper's own test (p ≤ 0.10); by the stricter p ≤ 0.05, texture at week 4 and age spots at week 12 were significant ([Aldag et al., 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5108505/)).
/figures/2/note: Three parts per million (0.0003%) of palmitoyl pentapeptide-4. No skin irritation was reported, and water loss through the skin did not differ between the two sides.
/glance/rows/0/v: Randomised, double-blind, split-face trial: each woman used both moisturisers, one on each side of the face, with the side chosen at random.
/glance/rows/1/v: 93 healthy Caucasian women aged 35 to 55 with fine lines and wrinkles on the face.
/glance/rows/2/v: An oil-in-water facial moisturiser with 3 ppm palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, about 0.4 g on one side of the face twice a day, after a two-week washout.
/glance/rows/3/v: The same moisturiser without the peptide, on the other side of the same face. Neither the women nor the graders knew which side had which.
/glance/rows/4/v: 12 weeks, with photographs at the start and at weeks 4, 8 and 12.
/glance/rows/5/v: Computer analysis of standardised photographs (lines around the eyes, texture on the cheeks), blinded expert grading of the two sides, the women's own ratings, and water loss through the skin.
/glance/rows/6/v: 3 ppm palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (0.0003%), stated in the abstract: the peptide itself, within the 2–8 ppm range recommended for cosmetics.
/glance/rows/7/v: All six authors were scientists at Procter & Gamble's Miami Valley Laboratories, and P&G sells skincare containing this peptide, so the trial is not independent.
/glance/rows/8/v: A — randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled and measured by image analysis and blinded graders; a small effect, with no size given in any source we could read.
/measurements/chart/title: Check-ups at which the peptide side was ahead of placebo
/measurements/chart/subtitle: Out of three check-ups (weeks 4, 8 and 12), by the paper's own test (p ≤ 0.10) and by the stricter, usual test (p ≤ 0.05). A count of check-ups, not the size of the change, which no readable source reports.
/measurements/chart/caption: By the paper's own test (p ≤ 0.10), the palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 side was ahead on skin texture at weeks 4 and 8, on fine lines and wrinkles at weeks 8 and 12, and on the look of age spots and dark circles at week 12. By the stricter, usual test (p ≤ 0.05), texture at week 4 and age spots at week 12 were significant. Timings from a review of the full paper (Aldag et al., 2016).
/media/alt: A soft peak of white moisturiser on a deep teal surface
/media/body/0: Ninety-three women aged 35 to 55 were given two facial moisturisers after a two-week washout: one with 3 ppm palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 and one without it, otherwise identical. Each applied about 0.4 g of one to the left side of her face and the other to the right, twice a day for 12 weeks, with the side decided at random and hidden from her and from the assessors.
/media/body/1: Faces were photographed at the start and at weeks 4, 8 and 12 with Procter & Gamble's REAL facial imaging system. Computers measured the lines around the eyes and the texture of the cheeks, expert graders compared the two sides of each face without knowing which was which, the women rated their own skin, and water loss through the skin was checked.
/limits/items/0: Which peptide this is. Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, the original Matrixyl®, not the two peptides of Matrixyl® 3000, whose own studies are on the [Matrixyl® 3000 evidence hub](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/matrixyl-3000-research).
/limits/items/1: How it was judged. Computer analysis of standardised photographs and expert graders working blind agreed, and the women's own ratings of their fine lines pointed the same way.
/limits/items/2: How big the effect was. The authors call it small, and significant at weeks 8 and 12. The full paper is paywalled and no source we could read gives a percentage, so this page reports when the differences appeared, not their size.
/limits/items/3: What “significant” means here. By the usual bar (p ≤ 0.05), the peptide side was ahead on skin texture at week 4 and on the look of age spots at week 12. The fine-line and wrinkle results met the paper's own, looser bar of p ≤ 0.10 ([Aldag et al., 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5108505/)).
/limits/items/4: Who took part. 93 Caucasian women aged 35 to 55; men and other ethnic groups were not included. The peptide was well tolerated, with no skin irritation reported.
/limits/items/5: Who ran it. All six authors worked for Procter & Gamble, which sells skincare containing this peptide. The paper was peer-reviewed and published in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science.
/context/heading: Where this trial sits in the evidence
/context/body/0: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 was designed from a piece of type I procollagen to prompt collagen production, and this trial tested whether it changes how facial skin looks. A 2011 academic review found it was then the only published human study to test the peptide apart from other actives ([Abu Samah and Heard, 2011](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-2494.2011.00657.x)).
/context/body/1: In Sederma's own two-month comparison, summarised by the independent Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel, creams with 3% Matrixyl® and 3% Matrixyl® 3000 both reduced deep wrinkles and roughness from the start, with no significant difference between them ([CIR, 2012](https://www.cir-safety.org/sites/default/files/palmit072012slr.pdf)). The same panel assessed palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 as safe in cosmetics as used, citing this trial's tolerance result ([CIR, 2024](https://www.cir-safety.org/sites/default/files/FR_Pentapeptides_092024.pdf)).
/context/body/2: Every study behind [Matrixyl® 3000](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/matrixyl-3000-research), the pair of peptides in our serum and cream, is graded on its evidence hub, alongside our other [ingredient research](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/the-science). The [Clinical studies](https://www.skingenetix.com/blogs/clinical-studies) list gathers every trial we have appraised.
/faq/questions/0: Does this trial prove the ingredient works?
/faq/questions/1: What concentration did the study use?
/faq/questions/3: Do Skingenetix products reproduce this result?
/faq/answers/0: It is the largest published controlled trial of palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 on its own: in 93 women, the peptide side improved more on fine lines and wrinkles than the placebo side from week 8, by image analysis and expert grading. The effect was small, and the trial tested the original Matrixyl®, not Matrixyl® 3000 (see its [evidence hub](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/matrixyl-3000-research)).
/faq/answers/1: 3 ppm (three parts per million, or 0.0003%) of palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 in an oil-in-water facial moisturiser, about 0.4 g per side twice a day. That is the peptide itself; a percentage on a label usually refers to a supplier's solution, which holds the peptide in parts per million.
/faq/answers/2: It was run by six Procter & Gamble scientists and published in the peer-reviewed International Journal of Cosmetic Science. P&G sells skincare containing this peptide, so it is not independent. A Cardiff University review later set out its design and results in detail ([Abu Samah and Heard, 2011](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-2494.2011.00657.x)).
/faq/answers/3: Our [Matrixyl 3000 Firming Serum](https://www.skingenetix.com/products/matrixyl-3000-firming-serum) contains palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 alongside Matrixyl® 3000; our [Pro-Collagen Firming Cream](https://www.skingenetix.com/products/matrixyl-3000-pro-collagen-firming-cream) contains Matrixyl® 3000 but not this peptide. The serum is a different formula from the trial's moisturiser, so its results are not the trial's results: we cite the trial for the ingredient as studied.
/meaning/heading: What it means for our products
/meaning/body/0: This trial is the main human evidence for the palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 in our serum: in a double-blind test in 93 women, the original Matrixyl® peptide reduced the look of fine lines and wrinkles more than the same moisturiser without it, from week 8.
/meaning/body/1: Our [Matrixyl 3000 Firming Serum](https://www.skingenetix.com/products/matrixyl-3000-firming-serum) pairs it with Matrixyl® 3000, whose own studies are on the [Matrixyl® 3000 research hub](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/matrixyl-3000-research). The serum is a different formula from the trial's moisturiser, so we cite the trial for the ingredient as studied, not as a result our serum has repeated.
